A strong arctic cold front moved through Oklahoma on Sunday November 24th.  Temperatures that had been in the 60s and 70s on Saturday fell into the 20s by Sunday evening.  Precipitation began as rain early Sunday morning then changed to sleet then freezing rain then finally to snow as the temperatures plummeted and the cold air pushed farther south.  Ice accumulated up to 1/2 inch thick mainly southeast of a line from Shawnee to Chickasha to Frederick, with ice up to 1 inch thick from Holdenville to Ada to Ardmore and southeastward.  Damage across southeastern and southcentral Oklahoma was severe. Power was out to a large portion of the area due to icing of power lines and tree limbs.  Electric companies throughout southcentral and southeastern Oklahoma estimated that over 152,000 people were without power at some time during the storm.  It took as long as 3 days to restore power to some customers. Bryan County was particularly hard-hit by ice up to 1 inch thick.  Telephone and power services were out almost countywide, including in Durant, Calera, Colbert, Cartwright, Caddo, and Bokchito.  Officials in Durant reported that trees and limbs were down on every block in town.  An old peanut dryer building collapsed in Bokchito due to the weight of the ice.  A radio station was forced off the air when its transmitter was covered with 2 to 3 inches of ice.  A second 500-foot radio tower fell near Lake Texoma due to the weight of the accumulated ice.  Carter County reported similar troubles, with power outages and numerous limbs and trees down in Ardmore, Lone Grove, Oilpatch, Ringling, Fox, Healdton, and Wilson. In Pushmataha County, a 190-foot microwave tower used by OETA to transmit public television collapsed due to the weight of ice.  The tower, which was located in a wooded area between Tuskahoma and Clayton, was completely destroyed. Trees, limbs, and power poles were broken by the weight of the ice throughout southeastern and southcentral Oklahoma.  Jefferson County reported 6 power poles broken west of Ringling and over 100 poles fell in Stephens and Cotton Counties east and south of Comanche and northeast and southeast of Marlow.Officials in Pontotoc County reported 20 poles and numerous trees and limbs down around the county with the worst damage in Fitzhugh.  Seminole County also suffered broken poles, crossarms, trees, and limbs.

A slow moving low pressure system, that moved from Williamsburg Virginia the morning of the 13th to about 100 miles southeast of Atlantic City the morning of the 14th and then drifted southeast to about 300 miles southeast of Atlantic City the morning of the 15th, and a high pressure system anchored over Quebec Province Canada produced a costant onshore flow for a couple of days.  This was augmented by the astronomical spring tides around the new moon.  Moderate tidal flooding occurred the morning of the 13th.  Minor tidal flooding persisted mainly during the higher morning high tides through the 15th.  The greatest tidal departures averaged about 2.5 feet above normal.  The high tides at Atlantic City reached 7.5 feet above mean low water the morning of the 13th, 7.1 feet above mean low water the morning of the 14th and 6.8 feet above mean low water the morning of the 15th.  The high tides at the Cape May Ferry Terminal reached 8.0 feet above mean low water the morning of the 13th, 7.3 feet above mean low water the morning of the 14th and 7.4 feet above mean low water the morning of the 15th.  The persistent east to northeast flow caused most of the moderate flooding the morning of the 13th to occur around the back bays as the water was unable to escape between high tide cycles. In Monmouth County, tidal flooding and road closures occurred around the Shrewsbury River in Sea Bright.  In Ocean County, back bay flooding inundated Ship Bottom's Central Avenue from 26th through 29th Streets.  In Atlantic County, a one mile stretch of the Black Horse Pike (U.S. Routes 40 and 322) was closed between Atlantic City and Pleasantville the morning of the 13th.  The westbound lanes were reopened that afternoon,  but the eastbound lanes remained closed all day. In Absecon, flooding forced the closure of U.S. Route 9 and Shore Road and caused three-hour-long traffic backups.  Other street closures due to flooding occurred in Atlantic City (the west side), Brigantine, Margate and Ventnor.    In Cape May County, tidal flooding forced the closure of New Jersey State Route 47 in Wildwood as well as Park Boulevard. In North Wildwood Spruce Avenue and the west end of town were flooded.  Five motorists were rescued from their submerged vehicles. Eight blocks in Ocean City were closed due to flooding.  The tidal flooding forced open manhole covers on 9th Street.  Dune Road was closed in Avalon.  Three roads were barricaded and closed through Saturday morning in Cape May City.  In West Cape May, the Cape Island Creek overflowed forcing the closure of the Leaming/Elmira Street Bridge.  Low lying flooding was reported around Schellenger's Landing in Lower Township.  Beach erosion occurred at the Cape May Point State Park and snow fencing was destroyed in Stone Harbor.   No significant property damage was reported.

A vigorous upper-level disturbance combined with available moisture and marginally cold air to produce a swath of heavy, wet snow across much of western Virginia from the Blue Ridge through the highlands, including most of the Shenandoah Valley.  Accumulations were highly dependent on elevation.  In general, western counties with mean elevations above 750 feet received 4 or 5 inches.  However, many locations above 2500 feet received 6 or more inches of snow.The snow, which accumulated in a 3 to 4 hour period, covered many area highways, resulting in numerous accidents.  Two particularly hard-hit counties were Augusta and Rockingham.  The road problems were exacerbated by the fact that this was the first major snow of the season; few, if any, abrasives had been previously applied.  The event, which arrived at the tail end of the evening commute, snarled traffic and induced dozens of accidents.  A woman was killed when her vehicle flipped on icy roads in Craigsville (VAZ025).  Numerous accidents involved multiple vehicles.  Damage from the storm was minimal; only a few power outages were reported by Virginia Power and the Rappahannock Electric Cooperative.

Snow amounts ranging from 1 to 3 inches fell across portions of north Georgia. No major travel problems were encountered because road temperatures were still warm enough to melt most of the snow as it made contact.

A strong arctic cold front moved through Oklahoma on Sunday November 24th.  Temperatures that had been in the 60s and 70s on Saturday fell into the 20s by Sunday evening.  Precipitation began as rain early Sunday morning then changed to sleet then freezing rain then finally to snow as the temperatures plummeted and the cold air pushed farther south.  Ice accumulated up to 1/2 inch thick mainly southeast of a line from Shawnee to Chickasha to Frederick, with ice up to 1 inch thick from Holdenville to Ada to Ardmore and southeastward.  Damage across southeastern and southcentral Oklahoma was severe. Power was out to a large portion of the area due to icing of power lines and tree limbs.  Electric companies throughout southcentral and southeastern Oklahoma estimated that over 152,000 people were without power at some time during the storm.  It took as long as 3 days to restore power to some customers. Bryan County was particularly hard-hit by ice up to 1 inch thick.  Telephone and power services were out almost countywide, including in Durant, Calera, Colbert, Cartwright, Caddo, and Bokchito.  Officials in Durant reported that trees and limbs were down on every block in town.  An old peanut dryer building collapsed in Bokchito due to the weight of the ice.  A radio station was forced off the air when its transmitter was covered with 2 to 3 inches of ice.  A second 500-foot radio tower fell near Lake Texoma due to the weight of the accumulated ice.  Carter County reported similar troubles, with power outages and numerous limbs and trees down in Ardmore, Lone Grove, Oilpatch, Ringling, Fox, Healdton, and Wilson. In Pushmataha County, a 190-foot microwave tower used by OETA to transmit public television collapsed due to the weight of ice.  The tower, which was located in a wooded area between Tuskahoma and Clayton, was completely destroyed. Trees, limbs, and power poles were broken by the weight of the ice throughout southeastern and southcentral Oklahoma.  Jefferson County reported 6 power poles broken west of Ringling and over 100 poles fell in Stephens and Cotton Counties east and south of Comanche and northeast and southeast of Marlow.Officials in Pontotoc County reported 20 poles and numerous trees and limbs down around the county with the worst damage in Fitzhugh.  Seminole County also suffered broken poles, crossarms, trees, and limbs.

Low pressure tracking through extreme southeast Wisconsin brought heavy snow to the east central and northeast parts of the state, making holiday travel difficult and disrupting last minute Christmas shopping excursions.  The heaviest snow, with accumulations of 9 to 12 inches, fell in a 30 to 40 mile wide band extending from Redgranite (Waushara county) to Marinette (Marinette county).  This area received heavy convective snow bursts on the evening of the 23rd, with snowfall rates exceeding 2 inches per hour at times.  Thunder was reported in Green Bay.  The greatest snowfall reported was one foot in Hortonville (Outagamie county), followed by 11.5 inches in Appleton (Outagamie county) and 10 inches at the National Weather Service office in Green Bay.  Six to eight inch amounts were measured across most other parts of east central and northeast Wisconsin, except near the Lake Michigan shoreline, where warmer temperatures resulted in a mixture of rain and snow.  North winds gusting as high as 30 mph caused considerable blowing and drifting of the newly fallen snow, leading to near-blizzard conditions at times.

A slow moving low pressure system moved from Williamsburg, Virginia the morning of the 13th to about 100 miles southeast of Atlantic City the morning of the 14th and then drifted southeast to about 300 miles southeast of Atlantic City the morning of the 15th.  A prolonged period of rain and snow fell across the area.  As precipitation increased in intensity, it changed over to heavy snow during the evening of the 13th and lasted through the morning of the 14th.  Accumulations were as high as six inches in Carbon County and ranged from three inches in the valleys to close to a foot over the higher terrain in Monroe County.Once again Monroe County was hit the hardest as heavy wet snow took down trees and power lines.  About 6,000 Pennsylvania Power and Light customers lost power in Brodheadsville, Henryville, Lake Naomi and Stroudsburg.  About 5,000 General Public Utilities customers lost power in Cherry Valley, Delaware Water Gap, Saylorsburg, Stroud Township and Syndersville.  Full power was not restored until the 15th. The combination of snow and rain dropped about two to 3.5 inches of precipitation over a 48 hour period in the area.  Precipitation totals included 3.32 inches in East Stroudsburg and 1.91 inches in Jundale. To date Stroudsburg broke its all-time yearly precipitation record amassing 68.03 inches so far in 1996.  The previous record was 65.83 inches.
Sheriff's office reported Highway 41 with 3 to 4 feet of water. One car was partially submerged.

A strong upper-level jet streak induced lift of residual low-level moisture into polar air, producing two separate batches of light snow which totaled an average of 4 inches or more in portions of the central Shenandoah Valley.  Elevations above 2500 feet received between 4 and 8 inches of snow; elevations below 1000 feet received less than 4 inches.  Schools closed on the 20th in Shenandoah and Augusta Cos (VAZ025-027), giving children and extended winter break.  Most of the snow accumulated on grassy surfaces and trees.

Strong low pressure system which deposited heavy snow over much of Minnesota on 12/23/96, pulled extremely cold Canadian air southward over Minnesota on 12/24 and 12/25.  The cold remained entrenched through 12/26.  Temperatures fell to 15 to 35 degrees below zero  Christmas Day morning and Thursday morning.  The Twin Cities and St. Cloud set new record low temperatures both days.  In addition, the high temperature on Christmas Day in the Twin Cities was only 9 degrees below zero.  Combined with the record low temperature that morning of 22 below, the mean temperature for Christmas Day was 16 degrees below zero.  Christmas Day, 1996 set a new record for being the coldest day on record for the Twin Cities metro area going back to when modern day records began in 1890.  The next morning, the Twin Cities fell to 27 degrees below zero while St. Cloud plummeted to 34 below.  Wild River State Park in Chisago County measured a temperature of 38 below.

Widespread damage occurred to electrical poles and lines, leaving thousands without power for up to four days. Numerous accidents occurred, including many vehicles which slid off the road. One fatality occurred in a semi accident on Interstate 90 near Plankinton on November 14th. Two fatalities occurred 9 miles south of Coleman when a car slid off a gravel road and into a stream, drowning the occupants, also on November 14th. A school bus slid into a ditch near Lennox on November 18th, causing four minor injuries. Several injuries due to falls were reported in the Sioux Falls area. Many surfaces were coated with more than an inch of ice, making gravel roads as slippery as paved roads. Tree damage was widespread with tree debris blocking several roads and siedwalks. Some farm buildings and other small structures were damaged by the weight of ice and snow on roofs. Damage continued past the ending of the ice storm, including some damage when ice melted unevenly during later milder weather. The total extent of the damage was expected to be unknown for a long period.

Accumulations were highly dependent on elevation.  In general, western counties with mean elevations above 750 feet received 4 or 5 inches.  However, many locations above 2500 feet received 6 or more inches of snow.The snow, which accumulated in a 3 to 4 hour period, covered many area highways, resulting in numerous accidents.  Two particularly hard-hit counties were Augusta and Rockingham.  The road problems were exacerbated by the fact that this was the first major snow of the season; few, if any, abrasives had been previously applied.  The event, which arrived at the tail end of the evening commute, snarled traffic and induced dozens of accidents.  A woman was killed when her vehicle flipped on icy roads in Craigsville (VAZ025).  Numerous accidents involved multiple vehicles.  Damage from the storm was minimal; only a few power outages were reported by Virginia Power and the Rappahannock Electric Cooperative.

A two-day blizzard brought two to four inches of snow and wind gusts over 60 mph to Western South Dakota.  Numerous traffic accidents were caused by blowing and drifting snow.  One vehicle flipped off a bridge on Interstate-90 near Wasta; the driver was hospitalized in critical condition.  Forty-four people were rescued from vehicles stranded along roads.  Many highways, including the Interstate, were closed.  Homes and streets in the Buffalo, Lemmon, and Faith areas were covered by ten foot snow drifts.  Numerous livestock were missing after wandering off during the storm.

Cold air settled in over relatively warm ground resulting in the formation of dense fog. An arctic cold front plunged into North Central Texas during the morning hours of the 17th causing surface temperatures to fall rapidly into the 20s. An upper level disturbance approached northern Texas from the west as the arctic air deepened over the area. As the disturbance moved into the southern plains, precipitation developed across the northern portion of North Central Texas and fell to the ground in the form of snow. Accumulations were generally light but some locations north of a Jacksboro to Denton to Sulphur Springs line received as much as one inch of snow during the afternoon and evening hours. Automobiles compacted and melted the snow that accumulated on road surfaces. Because temperatures were well below freezing the moisture refroze on bridges and overpasses in many of the locations that received the heavier snowfall. Icy conditions resulted in numerous traffic accidents and a few indirect injuries. The most notable icing problems were reported in Hopkins, Montague, Hunt, Lamar and Fannin Counties.

Heavy snow from a synoptic system rapidly became lake enhanced and dumped storm totals up to 20 inches in central Ottawa and VanBuren counties.  Widespread reports of 12 inches were common throughout all the Lake Michigan shoreline counties from northern Berrien County to Oceana County.  Schools were closed for up to 2 days in some areas.  Some secondary roads were blocked until road crews could get control of the situation.  Some business and industry operated with reduced personnel and shifts on the 19th.

A powerful Alberta Clipper and a slow moving deep Arctic high pressure brought widespread prolonged blizzard conditions to Big Stone and Traverse counties. The clipper dropped from 2 to 4 inches of snowfall on top of the already expansive and deep snow cover of 1 to 2 feet. Conditions deteriorated throughout the afternoon of the 16th, with a full fledged blizzard by the morning of the 17th. North winds of 30 to 40 mph gusting to 50 mph brought visibilities to near zero and caused heavy drifting, making travel impossible. All schools were closed for several days. Some people had to be rescued from their vehicles after getting stuck in big snowdrifts or going into the ditch because of poor visibilities. Farmers and ranchers had problems getting feed to their livestock. Mail was delayed for some people up to several days with a backup of Christmas packages. Most roads were closed or blocked from the huge snowdrifts, leaving some people stranded to wait out the storm. Snowplows had an extremely difficult time because they could not see the road or the roads would become drifted over a short time after they were plowed. There were some accidents with mainly minor injuries. Many emergency personnel and road crews were working extended hours to keep up with the storm. All sports and other activities were canceled or postponed.

In a similar occurrence to what transpired during the morning of the 6th, precipitation spread across Sussex County by early afternoon on the 7th.  Precipitation type became elevation dependent. Snowfall accumulations averaged around 2 inches in the valleys and as high as around 7 inches over the higher terrain in the northwest part of the county.  Representative accumulations included 7 inches at High Point and Wantage, 5 inches in Hainesville and 2 inches in Newton.

Strong northeast winds occurred elsewhere in eastern Massachusetts, especially along the coast.  A peak gust to 85 knots was reported offshore on Georges Bank.  Very heavy snowfalls were reported from the higher terrain in the central and western part of the state.  A maximum total of 18 inches was measured at Worthington at an elevation of 1,433 feet in the Berkshires in western Hampshire County.  Springfield, at an elevation of about 100 feet, had less than 3 inches.  Six inches of snow was reported from Westfield.  The snow was heavy and wet, causing scattered power outages throughout central and western Massachusetts and it resulted in outages affecting up to 1,000 customers in the west and southwest suburbs of Boston. Easterly wind gusts reached 63 mph at Middleton Island Tuesday in advance of the front.  Gusts from 50 to 60 mph were reported near Cordova and at several buoys in and near Prince William Sound Tuesday. While airline flights were able to depart as scheduled that evening, many persons had difficulty reaching the Dubuque airport and missed their flights.

Arctic air crossing the warm waters of Lake Erie produced a narrow intense band of lake effect snow. Snowfall rates of two to three inches an hour were common in the band. Parts of the New York State Thruway were closed for more than 12 hours. Thirty to forty cars were stranded near Angola. A winter storm began on Christmas Eve in Western Idaho.  Heavy snow fell overnight, Cottonwood received 18 inches and 10-11 inches fell in Valley and Boise counties.  On Christmas day, 6 to 9 inches fell in the Lewiston area, 9 inches fell at Grangeville, and 6 inches fell at Coeur d'Alene.  The power was out most of the day in Northern Idaho.  As the storm progessed eastward, several highways in the southeast were closed due to snow and blowing snow.  Totals across Teton, Fremont and Bonneville counties ranged from 12 to 16 inches of snow.  On December 26th, blizzard conditions continued in Northern Idaho, the heavy snow closed the Lewiston airport, postal workers couldn't complete their routes for the first time in 28 years, and roads were closed.  In Nez Perce county, a county disaster was declared with nearly 2 feet of new snow falling.  In the Southwest, Bogus Basin Ski Resort near Boise, was closed due heavy snow toppling 150 trees.

An intensifying storm system moving eastward from the southeast tip of Long Island caused heavy, wet snow across Massachusetts to the west and north of Boston.  It was the first major nor'easter of the season and, in addition to the heavy snow, it brought high winds to Cape Cod and Nantucket Island.  Strong northeast winds occurred elsewhere in eastern Massachusetts, especially along the coast.  A peak gust to 85 knots was reported offshore on Georges Bank.  Very heavy snowfalls were reported from the higher terrain in the central and western part of the state.  A maximum total of 18 inches was measured at Worthington at an elevation of 1,433 feet in the Berkshires in western Hampshire County.  Springfield, at an elevation of about 100 feet, had less than 3 inches.  Six inches of snow was reported from Westfield.  The snow was heavy and wet, causing scattered power outages throughout central and western Massachusetts and it resulted in outages affecting up to 1,000 customers in the west and southwest suburbs of Boston.  Very poor road conditions were reported in parts of western and central Massachusetts.  Worcester had 10 inches of snow and some other totals included:  Maynard, 8.5 inches; West Townsend, 8.3 inches; Hopkinton, 8 inches; and E. Woburn, 6 inches.  Several inches of snow fell along the east coast at Hingham, while farther inland, over Bristol County, the National Weather Service in Taunton had 5 inches and Norton had 4 inches.  There were reports of "thundersnow" from Bridgewater, Foxboro, and Wrentham.Cape Cod and the Islands had heavy rain and strong winds with a peak gust  to 75 mph recorded at the airport control tower on Nantucket.  On the Cape, a peak gust to 64 mph was reported from Chatham.  Other peak wind gusts included:  Otis AFB, Falmouth, 61 mph; Plymouth, 50 mph; and Winthrop, 46 mph.

Strong south to southwest winds ahead of an approaching cold front reached sustained speeds of 25 to 35 mph with gusts to 40 to 50 mph.  The strong winds began around mid-morning and continued throughout the day and evening.  Power outages occurred in the Merrimack Valley, affecting up to 4,700 electric customers.  Peak wind gusts included: Boston, 47 mph; Worcester, 48 mph; Blue Hill, Milton, 61 mph; Chatham, 52 mph; and Easton, 39 mph.  Record high temperature readings occurred, with 61 degrees at Boston exceeding the old record of 60 in 1990.  Worcester tied their record of 57 degrees and Blue Hill Observatory in Milton set a record high of 58 degrees, surpassing the old record of 57 set in 1990.

An Alberta Clipper crossed eastern North Dakota, then stalled near Park Rapids, MN.  Before washing out, this strong low pressure system produced an intense pressure gradient, resulting in very strong north winds.  Fargo, ND, reported a peak wind of 47 mph on the 17th.  Although snowfall totals mostly ranged under 8 inches, snowdrifts up to 10 feet high were reported.  Many schools were cancelled for 2 days.  Interstate 94 was closed from Moorhead to Fergus Falls, US Highway 10 was closed from Moorhead to Wadena, and US Highway 2 was closed from East Grand Forks to Crookston.

The first winter storm of the year moved through Montana and slowed over North Dakota. Unseasonably warm air ahead of the low was replaced by cold arctic air. Snow began falling in the western part of the state on the evening of Sunday, Oct. 20th and continued into the morning of the 21st. 2 injuries were reported during the winter storm near Williston in an auto accident. The ages of those involved were not reported, nor were the extent of their injuries. The heaviest snow reported with the storm was 6 inches at Bowman, Williston and Berthold. 4 inches of snow fell at Minot. North winds up to 35 mph also created the first below zero wind chill values of the season. The winds also hampered travel with blowing snow and visibilities down to less than 1/4 mile. No road closures were reported however.

A narrow band of heavy snow, only about 25 miles wide, extended from Carbondale northeastward through Mt. Vernon. Maximum totals in this band were from 5 to 7 inches, including 5 inches at Carbondale and 7 inches in northwest Hamilton County. The surprise snowstorm gave thousands of students the day off from school. Numerous vehicles slid off roads, but no injuries or major damage was reported. Local hardware stores quickly sold out of winter supplies. The storm began as rain, then changed briefly to sleet and freezing rain before turning to heavy snow.

Lightning struck a home in Redfield and damaged the computer, satellite dishes and receivers, stereo system, television, VCR, telephones, and answering machine. The microwave, cameras, truck compass, and some electrical plugs-ins were also damaged. The phone connector box cover was blown off the side of the house into the middle of the yard. Telephone cords were all black and some were in several pieces.

A coastal storm which was fed tropical moisture by the circulation  around Hurricane Lily produced between 4 and 19 inches of rain throughout the County during a 30-hour period.  Many homes and businesses were flooded.  Many roads and bridges were washed out.  The city of Portland was without potable water for 24 hours as 4 major water mains were broken.  One man drowned when the man  and his wife attempted to drive across a flooded roadway that had been washed out.  An area dam failed.

A cold front moving southward through west Texas was a focus for severe thunderstorm development during the evening hours.  The dry line limited the western extent of the development.  A strong southwest flow aloft and low level dew points in the lower 60s made for a promising late-season severe weather event.  Most of the convection formed into a long squall line that stretched from near Snyder to Sanderson, but two cells formed ahead of the line in Reagan County and became supercells.  Also at the end of the line a supercell tracked across Sanderson where tennis ball size hail fell.

A fast-moving, very strong winter storm system blew through Utah wreaking havoc with the heavy travel at the end of the Thanksgiving weekend.   Gusty winds combined with periods of heavy snow to create local blizzard conditions.  Winds gusted from 30-40 mph.   Snowfall amounts were 3-7 inches in the valleys and 10-18 inches in the mountains.  The highest totals were in Filmore with 7 inches (valleys) and at several northern ski resorts with 18 inches (mountains).  Over 150 traffic accidents were reported statewide during this storm. In Fillmore the Utah National Guard was forced to allow about 70 stranded motorists to spend the night in its armory.  All 7 motels in the area were already filled to capacity.

Another round of heavy snow hit most of the Puget Sound area.  At 430 am Port Angeles had 15" new snow and 25" on the ground.  In North Seattle the snow changed to rain at 6 am, but by that time they had 9" new snow and 22" on the ground.  Friday Harbor had 12" overnight and a snow depth of 30".  Silverdale 10" new snow and 21" total.  By 8 am Hoodsport was raining, but overnight they received 13" and had 28" on the ground.  By 9 am, when most of the snow turned to rain, most places around Puget Sound had 18 to 24 inches of snow on the ground.  Nearly every county in Western Washington was declared a disaster, with nearly $100 million in damage in King County alone.  Numerous marina boat shelters collapsed under the weight of heavy snow, sinking nearly 400 boats and causing about $8 million worth of damage.  Bus service in Seattle was cancelled for the first time ever.  76 roads or state highways were closed at one point.  There were many power outages and dozens of collapsed roofs.  Mail and paper deliveries were held up.  There was approximately $225 million in insured damage over western WA.  Kenneth Schmoe, of Issaquah, was killed by a tree branch.  There was also one car accident death that was not directly related to the heavy snow. In Gig Harbor some people were without power for four to five days.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A moist westerly flow brought more snow to the mountains of western Colorado.  The heaviest snowfall occurred near the Continental Divide, with 6 to 12 inches common.  At least 15 inches of new snow fell in the mountains around Vail.  Winds were clocked in excess of 50 mph in many areas producing blowing and drifting snow.  A gust to 81 mph was observed on the peaks above Snowmass.

A slow moving low pressure system moved from the central Ohio Valley the morning of the 12th to Williamsburg, Virginia the morning of the 13th, to about 100 miles southeast of Atlantic City the morning of the 14th, then drifted southeast and was about 300 miles southeast of Atlantic City the morning of the 15th.  This produced about 48 hours of continuous rain from the evening of the 12th through the evening of the 14th.  Rain became heavy at times during the night of the 13th through the morning of the 14th.  Rain mixed with snow at times during the morning of the 14th over some of the higher terrain of Northwest New Jersey.  Accumulation averaged around two inches in Wantage, Newton and Vernon.  Storm totals averaged between one and four inches with the lowest amounts in Sussex County and the highest amounts in the southwest part of the state.   Since the rain was spread over an extended period of time, flooding was mainly confined to urban and poor drainage areas.  Basement flooding did occur, with the highest reports in Burlington County.  The heavy rain also damaged a bridge over the Cranbury Creek in Plainsboro (Middlesex County).  Precipitation totals included 4.28 inches in Pennsauken (Camden County),  3.89 inches in Verga (Gloucester County), 2.61 inches in New Lisbon (Burlington County), 2.49 inches in Mount Holly (Burlington County), 2.00 inches in Estell Manor (Atlantic County), 1.93 inches in Belvidere (Warren County), 1.71 inches within Atlantic City, 1.58 inches in New Brunswick (Middlesex County) and 1.37 inches in Newton (Sussex County).
Strong northwest winds combined with cold temperatures to produce wind chills of 35 to 45 below zero.

A strong upper level disturbance moved through the central plains and caused three to nine inches of snow across northeast Nebraska.  The highest snow amounts occurred in Antelope, Pierce, and Wayne counties.

A coastal storm moving northeastward from Virginia to Maine brought heavy snow to all except  the extreme southeast corner of the state.  Snowfall ranged from 6 inches in the Upper Connectticut River Valley to up to 16 inches in the central part of the state.  In southern areas, the wet, heavy snow downed numerous trees and power lines causing about one quarter of the state population to lose electrical power.  For some, the power outage lasted as much as five days.  This storm was the most extensive and costliest weather related power outage in the state's history.

The combination of some very light snow (for most the first snow of the season), road and air temperatures below freezing and heavy  traffic volume because of Thanksgiving Day caused roadways to become extremely slippery and hazardous, especially on bridges and overpasses.  Accumulations were less than an inch.  But that was enough to cause numerous accidents across the area.  Because of the holiday and the surprising roadway result of this light snow, it took a while for road crews to recover. Although the snow ended by 6 p.m. EDT, road conditions did not improve in some areas until 10 p.m EST. In Philadelphia, a 30-year-old woman died after losing control of her car and slammed into a tree. The Platt and Grays Ferry Bridges were closed from late afternoon until 9 p.m. EST.  By 5 p.m. EST all the major arteries within the city had slowed to a crawl.  In Chester County, two people were seriously injured in a four vehicle collision on a Pennsylvania State Route 100 bridge over the Schuylkill River.  The U.S. Route 30 Bypass had many accidents.  In West Goshen alone, emergency personnel responded to 43 accidents.  The Tredyffrin Police had to close the southbound lanes of U.S. Route 202.  In Delaware County, the Commodore Barry Bridge was closed due to icing until 9 p.m. EST.Pennsylvania State Route 309 was very icy in Bucks and Montgomery Counties.  Elsewhere in Montgomery County, portions of the Blue Route (Interstate 476) were closed as were the West Chester Pike over the Blue Route and U.S. Route 202 over the Dannehower Bridge.  Many accidents were reported on Pennsylvania State Route 29 from Schwenksville to Collegeville and along Germantown Pike and U.S. Route 422.In the Lehigh Valley, the worst problems were in Northampton County.  Travel was extremely treacherous along U.S. Route 22, Pennsylvania State Route 512 and over the Glendon Bridge.

A winter storm brought a mixture of rain, freezing rain, sleet, snow and strong winds to Central Illinois on November 25. This was the result of a strong low pressure system moving northeast from the lower Mississippi Valley combining with cold air pushing south on the back side of the low into Central Illinois. Significant icing occurred in this area. This caused numerous accidents and power outages. Several injuries were reported from the accidents but no deaths. Power outages came as ice covered power lines snapped from winds of 15 to 30 mph.

Heavy snow of 6 to 8 inches fell across most of northern South Dakota adding to the already significant snow depth. Roads became snowpacked which hampered travel resulting in the postponement of many activities. Some snowfall amounts include, 6 inches at Aberdeen, Mclaughlin, Isabel, Roscoe, and Mellette, 7 inches at Eagle Butte, Timber Lake, Selby, Faulkton, Leola, Frederick, Webster, and Sisseton, 8 inches at Britton, Ipswich, Eureka, and Mclaughlin.

An intense low pressure system tracked north of Lake Superior on the 30th, with its trailing cold front crossing southeast Michigan during the early morning hours.  High winds associated with the front did widespread damage.  Reports of damage began with the roof being torn off of a house in Ida, in Monroe county, shortly after midnight.  Through the day, high winds downed trees and powerlines, causing outages throughout southeast Michigan.  Detroit Edison reported outages to 70,000 customers.  In downtown Detroit, the high winds snapped a scaffolding cable on the Renaissance Center at around 730 am EDT, shattering 20 windowpanes and showering an atrium and parking lot with glass.  Elsewhere, large trees blew over, crashing through the roofs of houses at Detroit Beach in Monroe county and in Ann Arbor (Washtenaw county).

A deep low pressure moving east across Ontario Canada brought winds of 60 to 70 miles per hour, with higher gusts, to Northern Ohio.  Trees, limbs and power lines were downed, some across roads, and others on cars, and buildings causing considerable damage.  In Cuyahoga County, at Cleveland Hopkins Airport, a stewardess was blown off the steps of a commuter plane but was not injured.  At least 2 cars, a truck and a house were struck by falling trees in Bay Village and shingles were blown from roofs in Berea.  In Wayne County, signs were ripped from their standards and dropped on roads and a landfill was closed in Paint Township because of flying metal and tin.  At Apple Creek, the arc from wind whipped downed electrical wires leading to a barn may have ignited a fire which was then whipped into an inferno by the high winds.  The barn and some of the cattle in it were destroyed.  A 16 ton concrete wall at a Revco drugstore under construction in Akron in Summit County was toppled and, in Springfield Township, a storage facility under construction was destroyed.  Also in Summit County, a 45 year old man, was struck by a falling tree at Raintree Country Club and died of head injuries.  A wind gust of 67 miles per hour was reported at Kent in Portage County.  A wind gust of 79 miles per hour was reported at Fairport Harbor in Lake County.  A 71 mile per hour wind gust was reported in Ashtabula County, where a tree fell on a house in Geneva.  In Jackson Township in Mahoning County, a construction barrel was blown into the path of a car, causing the car to collide with a truck and a concrete wall on Interstate 80.  The driver of the car was treated for injuries.  A 68 mile per hour wind gust was reported at Toledo Express Airport in Lucas County.  On Interstate 75 near Bowling Green in Wood County, a wind gust caused a semi truck to veer left of center and sideswipe another rig.  There were no injuries.  Also in Bowling Green, at least one tree fell on a house, one tree fell on two cars and a dumpster landed on another car.  In Perrysburg Township, also in Wood County, the Islamic Center of Toledo was damaged when two minarets on top of a building were toppled and in Liberty Township, a wind gust forced a car into a utility pole, slightly injuring the driver.  In Sandusky County, corn stalks that had been injured by corn borers, were very susceptible to the high winds.  The loss to the corn crop was estimated at 10 to 30 percent.  In Washington Township in Richland County, half the roof was blown from a barn, crumpled, and scattered across a road and a field.  Tin strips dangled like confetti from what was left of the roof.

Also in Summit County, a 45 year old man, was struck by a falling tree at Raintree Country Club and died of head injuries.  A wind gust of 67 miles per hour was reported at Kent in Portage County.  A wind gust of 79 miles per hour was reported at Fairport Harbor in Lake County.  A 71 mile per hour wind gust was reported in Ashtabula County, where a tree fell on a house in Geneva.  In Jackson Township in Mahoning County, a construction barrel was blown into the path of a car, causing the car to collide with a truck and a concrete wall on Interstate 80.  The driver of the car was treated for injuries.  A 68 mile per hour wind gust was reported at Toledo Express Airport in Lucas County.  On Interstate 75 near Bowling Green in Wood County, a wind gust caused a semi truck to veer left of center and sideswipe another rig.  There were no injuries.  Also in Bowling Green, at least one tree fell on a house, one tree fell on two cars and a dumpster landed on another car.  In Perrysburg Township, also in Wood County, the Islamic Center of Toledo was damaged when two minarets on top of a building were toppled and in Liberty Township, a wind gust forced a car into a utility pole, slightly injuring the driver.  In Sandusky County, corn stalks that had been injured by corn borers, were very susceptible to the high winds.  The loss to the corn crop was estimated at 10 to 30 percent.  In Washington Township in Richland County, half the roof was blown from a barn, crumpled, and scattered across a road and a field.  Tin strips dangled like confetti from what was left of the roof.

Clusters of strong thunderstorms developed in a moist unstable airmass ahead of a slow moving cold front.As thunderstorms moved east southeast at speeds averaging 20 MPH, they produced high winds, large hail and torrential rain.Trees were knocked down and a building collapsed at the intersection of Jersey and Front Streets in Port Jervis of Orange County.  In addition to the 1 inch diameter hail report from Stony Point, 3/4  inch diameter hail was also reported in Pomona in Rockland County.  Winds that gusted to 75  MPH downed trees in Ossining in Westchester County.  Serious flooding was reported along the Saw Mill River Parkway in Westchester County and across Southern New York County.  A huge maple tree was downed about 1/2 mile north of the Sayville train station in Suffolk County.

A line of severe thunderstorms developed in a moist unstable airmass along a cold front during the evening.As thunderstorms moved east at around 25 MPH, they caused damaging high winds and heavy rain.A funnel cloud was sighted in North Salem in Westchester County by the New York State Police.   Numerous trees and power lines were downed along and around Bloomer Road for about 1 mile in North Salem.Trees were also downed around Peach Lake in Putnam County.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A man sustained minor injury when struck by lightning.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm and unstable airmass was located over Iowa.  Surface dew point temperatures were surged into the lower to middle 70s ahead of an approaching cold front from the northwest.  The freezing level was quite high, over 14,000 feet MSL, thus hail was not a major problem.  Most of the storms were not severe, but rather heavy rain producers.  A few of the storms did become severe.  Nickel size hail fell northeast of Dallas in Marion County.  The storm had a VIL value from the WSR-88D of 80 kg/m/m.  High winds were reported in a few places.  Winds of nearly 70 MPH downed several trees in Union County at Lorimor.  Wind damage was also reported in Adams County at Corning.

Thunderstorms formed along a weak cold frontal boundary during the afternoon hours.  A cold pool of air aloft, with 500 mb temperatures around -12 C. was over the the area.  Though no severe thunderstorms occurred, there were numerous reports of cold air funnel clouds.
Wind gusts were clocked to 58 MPH at WSIL channel 3 near Marion. Numerous tree limbs were blown down in Marion.

Numerous large trees were blown down over a 2 block by 8 block area. A house, shed, and truck were damaged. The roof was blown off a mobile home. A National Weather Service damage survey indicated the damage was caused by a microburst with gusts near 70 MPH.

A winter storm moved through the state December 1-2.  In the Southeast, 5 to 16 inches of snow fell.  Sixteen inches of new snow fell at Victor in Teton county and twelve inches at Island Park in Fremont County.  Five to eight inches fell across Bannock, Bonneville, Caribou, Clark, Butte, Blaine and Power counties.

A storm dropped six to 12 inches of snow over northwest South Dakota.  The heaviest snow stretched from northeast Butte through northern Meade and Haakon counties.  Grand Electric Cooperative lost 268 poles in southern Perkins, Harding, northern Butte and Meade counties.  The damage was estimated at $194,000.  Numerous accidents occurred along Interstate 90, none with serious injuries.

Lake effect snowfalls over Minnesota's North Shore and Lakehead regions amounted to 22 inches at Two Harbors, 13 inches in Duluth, and 6 inches at Finland and Cloquet.

A coastal storm moving northeastward from Virginia to Maine brought heavy snow to all except  the extreme southeast corner of the state.  Snowfall ranged from 6 inches in the Upper Connectticut River Valley to up to 16 inches in the central part of the state.  In southern areas, the wet, heavy snow downed numerous trees and power lines causing about one quarter of the state population to lose electrical power.  For some, the power outage lasted as much as five days.  This storm was the most extensive and costliest weather related power outage in the state's history.
A moist Pacific Storm dumped heavy snow overnight on the Sierra Nevada mountains west of the Owens Valley.  Aspendell received at least 12 inches in less than 12 hours.
Moose Lodge in Elensburg collapsed from the weight of heavy snow.
A 48-year-old man was injured as he attempted to clear snow from a metal awning which then fell on him.
Snow slides close I-84 at times from Portland to The Dalles.
Fifty-one traffic accidents on ice covered highways.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Upto a foot of new snow caused at least 37 traffic accidents.  One woman suffered serious head and internal injuries when her car collided with a pickup.  Two others were treated and released.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Twenty-eight people taken to hospital after bus roll-over.

Low pressure moving northeastward from the mid-Atlantic States brought a mixture of precipitation to most of Maine.  In interior sections of coastal Maine, heavy accumulations of ice brought down numerous trees and caused widespread power outages.  Gusty winds also contributed to the damages as ice-laden trees and branches continued to fall after the precipitation had ended.  More than 60,000 customers lost electrical power.  Interior Cumberland County and Androscoggin County were particularly hard hit;  some people were without power for more than three days.

General 4 to 10 inch snowfall across much of the area.  Heaviest snowfalls of 6 to 10 inches in central and eastern sections of area while snow amounts were in the 4 to 6 inch range in the north.  A few snowfalls included 6 to 8 inches across the Twin Cities metro area, 10 inches in Jordan, 8 inches at Cambridge, Forest Lake, Hutchinson and Montevideo, and 6 inches at St. Cloud, Glenwood and Redwood Falls.  Strong winds of 20 to 30 mph in the wake of the storm on 12/24 resulted in restricted visibilities in blowing snow.  Highway 19 west of Redwood Falls, Highways 7 and 40 at Madison, and Highways 67 and 23 were closed out of Granite Falls. Her car was found Christmas Eve.  Her body was found in a snow covered field by a snowmobiler on 12/26.

The snow ended during the afternoon of the 25th.The highest snow totals were 20 inches at Two Heart (25 NNE of Newberry in Luce County), and 18 inches at Marquette and Calumet. A slow moving low pressure system moved from the central Ohio Valley the morning of the 12th to Williamsburg Virginia the morning of the 13th to about 100 miles east of Fenwick Island Delaware the morning of the 14th and then drifted southeast to about 275 miles southeast of Fenwick Island Delaware the morning of the 15th.  This produced about 48 hours of continuous rain from the evening of the 12th through the evening of the 14th.  Rain became heavy at times during the night of the 13th.  Storm totals averaged between two and three inches.  Since the rain was spread over an extended period of time, only some urban and poor drainage flooding occurred.  Precipitation totals included 3.76 inches at Newark Delaware, 2.85 inches at the Baltimore-Washington International Airport and 1.86 inches at Salisbury.

Persistent heavy rain moved over the county in squalls well before Hurricane FRAN made landfall. The broad center of the storm passed near the county before entering Virginia. The resulting tropical rains produced widespread flooding across the county.
Two separate storms in the late afternoon and early evening hours produced one to two inches of rain which resulted in widespread street flooding throughout the city.

Strong low pressure system which deposited heavy snow over much of Minnesota on 12/23/96, pulled extremely cold Canadian air southward over Minnesota on 12/24 and 12/25.  The cold remained entrenched through 12/26.  Temperatures fell to 15 to 35 degrees below zero  Christmas Day morning and Thursday morning.  The Twin Cities and St. Cloud set new record low temperatures both days.  In addition, the high temperature on Christmas Day in the Twin Cities was only 9 degrees below zero.  Combined with the record low temperature that morning of 22 below, the mean temperature for Christmas Day was 16 degrees below zero.  Christmas Day, 1996 set a new record for being the coldest day on record for the Twin Cities metro area going back to when modern day records began in 1890.  The next morning, the Twin Cities fell to 27 degrees below zero while St. Cloud plummeted to 34 below.  Wild River State Park in Chisago County measured a temperature of 38 below.

The precipitation began as snow around daybreak in the south but changed to sleet and freezing rain by late morning. Across central Indiana the precipitation remained mainly as snow. Snow accumulations ranged from 2 to 6 inches with amounts of 3 to 4 inches most common.  Though freezing rain did occur with this event it did not cause any significant power outages.

A strong arctic front blew through the state on this date.  High winds from the northeast developed as this front moved through.  Wind gusts from 70-110 mph were recorded from all the remote observing platforms in the mountains.  The highest wind gust measured was 111 mph on Baldy mountain at the Alta ski resort.  At a skiing event at the Deer Valley ski resort, a 12 foot metal judges' stand was blown over.  6 of the judges were injured in the incident.  Most of the state's ski lifts had to be closed.  These winds also surfaced in some valleys in eastern Utah as well.  Wind gusts estimated to be as high as 80 mph caused considerable damage in places.  In Emery windows were blown out af a van. Precipitation amounts ranged from about 4 inches above normal in Berks County to around 6.5 inches above normal in both Delaware and Monroe Counties. County average monthly precipitation totals ranged from 7.6 inches in Berks County to 10.3 inches in Monroe County.

A cold front moving from northwest to southeast brought strong southerly winds to all of the main Hawaiian Islands during December 26-27th.  Winds ranged from 35 to 45 mph with gusts estimated as high as 75  mph where the winds accelerated down the north facing slopes of the mountains on the islands of  Kauai, Oahu, Maui, and Hawaii.

An off-duty forecaster also measured a gust to 63 mph in Centerville.

A vigorous upper-level disturbance combined with available moisture and marginally cold temperatures to produce a swath of heavy wet snow across much of eastern West Virginia.  In general, accumulations were 4 or 5 inches, with only Grant Co (WVZ048) and Jefferson Co (WVZ053) receiving average accumulations of 3 inches.  The highest totals were in Pendleton Co (WVZ054), where 6 inches fell in Franklin, Sugar Grove, and Upper Tract.Totals exceeding 8 inches were likely at elevations above 2500 feet.

A vigorous upper-level disturbance combined with available moisture and marginally cold air to produce a swath of wet snow from the Maryland piedmont to the Potomac Highlands.  Only Allegany Co (MDZ002) received widespread accumulations of 4 inches or more; the remaining affected counties received average accumulations between 1 and 3 inches.Accumulations were highly dependent on elevation, especially in the foothills.  In Frederick Co (MDZ004), lower terrain received 2 or 3 inches.  However, along the western mountains, up to 9 inches may have fallen in Wolfsville.  The same was likely true in neighboring Washington (MDZ003) Co.  A similar effect occurred farther east, where 2 inches fell in western and northern Montgomery and Howard Cos (MDZ009>010), but plain rain fell in the southern and eastern portions.  In general, the dividing line of accumulating snow was at 750 feet above sea level.

Snowfall amounts of 7 to 12 inches occurred in the above mentioned areas.  The higher elevations of Delaware county saw the greatest accumulations, with Stamford picking up a foot of new snow and Meredith getting 10 inches.       The heavy wet nature of the snow downed trees and power lines throughout these regions.

December 1996 was the wettest December on record (1895-present) for New Jersey.  The statewide average of 7.9 inches surpassed the previous record of 7.29 inches set in 1973.  Precipitation amounts ranged from about 3.5 inches above normal in Middlesex County to 5.7 inches above normal in Warren County.  A new December precipitation record was set at nearby Philadelphia International Airport where 8.48 inches fell.  December 1996 was the second wettest on record at the Atlantic City International Airport (in Pomona) where 7.23 inches of precipitation fell.  December 1996 was the 8th wettest on record at the Marina in Atlantic City as 6.87 inches of rain fell.  County average rainfall totals ranged from 7.4 inches in Middlesex County to 9.2 inches in Hunterdon, Morris and Warren Counties.

The year 1996 was one of the wettest ones on record for Eastern Pennsylvania.  Precipitation amounts on a county average ranged from 59.5 inches in Lehigh County to a whopping 72.9 inches in Monroe County.  This was about 14 to 26 inches above normal.  It was the wettest year on record in Philadelphia as 56.47 inches of precipitation fell at the International Airport breaking the previous record of 55.28 inches set in 1973.  It also was the wettest year on record in Stroudsburg.  Other yearly precipitation totals included 74.45 inches in Exton (Chester County), 71.49 inches in Long Pond (Monroe County), 67.88 inches at Springtown (Bucks County), 63.96 inches in Spring House (Montgomery County) and 56.87 inches at the Lehigh Valley International Airport.

Hurricane Bertha slammed into the North Carolina coastline between Surf City and North Topsail Beach causing severe damage to property, utilities and roads.  Hardest hit were agricultural crops which suffered losses in excess of $126 million.  Heaviest damage was in Topsail Beach and all of Onslow County up the coast to Emerald Isle in Carteret County.  In Onslow alone, 199 structures were destroyed (117 were mobile homes).  An 8-10 foot storm surge struck Swansboro and Emerald Isle.  Several businesses were flooded.  Water flowed through the streets of Belhaven in Beaufort County where the surge was around 7 feet.  In New Bern, numerous boats were sunk or damaged at 3 private marinas.  Fishing piers were demolished all along the coast.  New River (Marine Corps Air Station in Jacksonville) reported a peak wind gust of 108 mph.  Rainfall across the region ranged from 8 inches in the Hofman Forest (Onslow) to 6 1/2 inches in Broad Creek to over 5 1/2 in Snow Hill and Washington.
Icy roads developed early in the morning following rain the previous day and evening resulting in numerous wrecks with some injuries (indirect).

Another round of heavy snow hit most of the Puget Sound area.  At 430 am Port Angeles had 15" new snow and 25" on the ground.  In North Seattle the snow changed to rain at 6 am, but by that time they had 9" new snow and 22" on the ground.  Friday Harbor had 12" overnight and a snow depth of 30".  Silverdale 10" new snow and 21" total.  By 8 am Hoodsport was raining, but overnight they received 13" and had 28" on the ground.  By 9 am, when most of the snow turned to rain, most places around Puget Sound had 18 to 24 inches of snow on the ground.  Nearly every county in Western Washington was declared a disaster, with nearly $100 million in damage in King County alone.  Numerous marina boat shelters collapsed under the weight of heavy snow, sinking nearly 400 boats and causing about $8 million worth of damage.  Bus service in Seattle was cancelled for the first time ever.  76 roads or state highways were closed at one point.  There were many power outages and dozens of collapsed roofs.  Mail and paper deliveries were held up.  There was approximately $225 million in insured damage over western WA.  Kenneth Schmoe, of Issaquah, was killed by a tree branch.  There was also one car accident death that was not directly related to the heavy snow. In Gig Harbor some people were without power for four to five days.

In addition, a wall of a building under contruction in Lafayette was toppled, a semi-truck was blown over near the Boulder turnpike damaging a concrete barrier, and a 60-ft tree crushed a parked pickup truck at a Denver residence.High wind reports from around the area included:  an estimated 120 mph (105 kts) at Blackhawk, 115 mph (100 kts) at Aspen Springs and 15 miles west of Fort Collins, and an estimated 110 mph (96 kts) 1 mile east of Buckhorn Mtn, 105 mph (91 kts) 2 1/2 miles north of Estes Park, 100 mph (87 kts) at Silver Spruce Ranch, 78 mph (68 kts) 9 miles west-northwest of Rustic, 75 mph (65 kts) atop Shanahan Ridge near Boulder, 74 mph (64 kts) 8 miles west of Conifer, and 71 mph (61 kts) at the Rocky Flats Environmental Test Facility.

For some, the power outage lasted as much as five days.  This storm was the most extensive and costliest weather related power outage in the state's history.

Strong low pressure system which deposited heavy snow over much of Minnesota on 12/23/96, pulled extremely cold Canadian air southward over Minnesota on 12/24 and 12/25.  The cold remained entrenched through 12/26.  Temperatures fell to 15 to 35 degrees below zero  Christmas Day morning and Thursday morning.  The Twin Cities and St. Cloud set new record low temperatures both days.  In addition, the high temperature on Christmas Day in the Twin Cities was only 9 degrees below zero.  Combined with the record low temperature that morning of 22 below, the mean temperature for Christmas Day was 16 degrees below zero.  Christmas Day, 1996 set a new record for being the coldest day on record for the Twin Cities metro area going back to when modern day records began in 1890.  The next morning, the Twin Cities fell to 27 degrees below zero while St. Cloud plummeted to 34 below.  Wild River State Park in Chisago County measured a temperature of 38 below.

Continued heavy snowpack caused more collapsed buildings, including many businesses and logging shops, Libby Middle School, and "Shed Six," the largest building in Lincoln County at more than 4 acres.  At least 37 buildings in Lincoln County alone fell under the weight of snow not including dozens of carports and other outbuildings.  One insurance company spokesman has estimated between $3 million and $4 million in insurance claims in Lincoln County.  Other buildings collapsed in Flathead and Sanders counties, and many others were saved through aggressive snow removal.  The snow removal bill for Tidyman's grocery store was $40,000 while costs throughout the area ran up to 3 times that of normal.

Low pressure produced 1 to 2 inches of rain across much of eastern New York during December 1 through the morning of December 2.  Rainfall totals around 3 inches occurred over parts of the upper Hudson River Basin and in the Catskills.  This amount of rainfall during the late fall season resulted in flooding across much of the region.  In Fulton County, the Cavadutta Creek flooded in the Town of Johnstown and flooding was also reported in the Caroga Lake area.  In Montgomery County, roads in low lying areas were flooded in the Towns of Florida, Palatine and Canajoharie.  State Highway 30 was flooded in the Town of Florida.  In Schoharie County, flooding occurred in the Towns of Cobleskill, Richmondville and Esperance.  In the Village of Cobleskill, West Street and Quarry Street were washed out.  Basements were flooded in Barnerville due to the Cobleskill Creek.  In the Town of Richmondville, Mickle Road and Warnerville Cutoff Road were closed.  Flooding was widespread in Ulster County.  Roads were closed in the Towns of Denning, Hardenburgh, New Paltz, Kingston, Ulster, Woodstock and Saugerties.  A state of emergency was declared in the Town of Shandaken during the morning hours of December 2.  McKinley Hollow Road and Lost Cove Road were severely damaged.  Old route 28 was flooded between Phoenicia and Mount Tremper.  The Town of Hardenburgh also suffered severe road damage.  In the Town of Woodstock, roads were flooded when the Sawkill overflowed its banks.  The Esopus Creek crested 2.5 feet above flood stage above the Ashokan Reservoir.  The lower Esopus Creek went approximately 3 feet over flood stage when water spilled over the top of the Ashokan Dam.  Orlando Street and Sandy Road in the Town of Ulster were evacuated along the Esopus Creek.  Damage was minor during this flooding event along the entire Esopus Creek.  In Hamlton County, the Sacandaga River went 2 feet above flood stage at Hope.  In Washington County, many roads were flooded and washed out.  In the Village of Whitehall, Broadway was closed for several hours.  In the Town of Fort Ann, Hogtown Road and Shelving Rock Road were badly washed out.  Many roads were also flooded and washed out in Warren County.  The Towns of Thurman, Bolton and Stony Creek were hardest hit.  State Highway 8 in the Town of Horicon, had a 30 foot section washed out across both lanes.  State Highway 9N in the Town of Bolton was closed until late afternoon on December 2.  The Mohawk River flooded in southern Herkimer County, Montgomery County and in Schenectady County.  The flooding was fairly minor.  The river went 1 foot above flood stage at Little Falls and crested near flood stage in Schenectady.  Roads at the industrial park near Little Falls were flooded.  In Montgomery County, the Tribes Hill Bridge in Fort Hunter was closed as a steel gate on Lock 12 under the bridge was forced open.  In Schenectday County, River Road was flooded in Niskayuna and some flooding occurred in the Stockade region in Schenectady.  Minor flooding occurred along the Schoharie Creek in Schoharie, Montgomery and western Schenectady Counties.  The creek reached the 6 foot flood stage at Burtonville in Montgomery County and some flooding occurred in the Lost Valley.  In Schoharie County, Redling and Bielfeldt Roads were flooded along the creek.  Minor flooding occurred along the Hoosic River in southern Washington County and northern Rensselaer County.  At Buskirk in Rensselaer County, Firehouse Road was closed between the covered bridge and County Route 67.  Minor flooding occurred along the Hudson River in Saratoga and Washington Counties.  Fort Edward in Washington County and Waterford and the Stillwater Flats in Saratoga County sustained minor flooding.  Along the Moose River in northern Herkimer County, minor flooding occurred at McKeever.  The West Canada Creek flooded in southern Herkimer County from the Hinckley Reservoir downsteam to the Mohawk River.  The flooding was confined to low lying areas.

A fast-moving, very strong winter storm system blew through Utah wreaking havoc with the heavy travel at the end of the Thanksgiving weekend.   Gusty winds combined with periods of heavy snow to create local blizzard conditions.  Winds gusted from 30-40 mph.   Snowfall amounts were 3-7 inches in the valleys and 10-18 inches in the mountains.  The highest totals were in Filmore with 7 inches (valleys) and at several northern ski resorts with 18 inches (mountains).  Over 150 traffic accidents were reported statewide during this storm.  Numerous power outages and tractor-trailer rollovers were reported.  "White-out conditions" occurred from Nephi to Cedar City on Interstate-15.  In Fillmore the Utah National Guard was forced to allow about 70 stranded motorists to spend the night in its armory.  All 7 motels in the area were already filled to capacity.

Total snowfall accumulations ranged from 12 to 24 inches over Oswego, Lewis and southern Jefferson counties. Portions of I-81 were closed. Numerous accidents were blamed on the heavy snow and whiteouts. Various activities had to be cancelled because of the snow.

A winter storm moving through the state on December 20th through the 21st produced heavy snow over much of the South.  Ten inches of snow fell at the Boise Air Terminal.  This became the 2nd highest total for a twenty-four hour event.  Other totals ranged from 5 to 8 inches across the entire South.  Some of the higher totals included:  9 inches at Garden Valley in Boise county and 8 inches in Elmore, Canyon, Cassia, Bannock, Teton, Caribou and Fremont counties.  Across the Pocatello area, including Blackfoot 6 to 8 inches of snow fell.

Heavy snow from a synoptic system rapidly became lake enhanced and dumped storm totals up to 20 inches in central Ottawa and VanBuren counties.  Widespread reports of 12 inches were common throughout all the Lake Michigan shoreline counties from northern Berrien County to Oceana County.  Schools were closed for up to 2 days in some areas.  Some secondary roads were blocked until road crews could get control of the situation.  Some business and industry operated with reduced personnel and shifts on the 19th.

A Pacific storm produced heavy rains and strong wind in the Sacramento and northern San Joaquin valleys. Snow accumulations in the mountains measured 10 inches at Lake Tahoe and 2.5 to 3 feet of snow at higher elevations. Minor flooding occurred in Solano county and in the city of Turlock (Stanislaus county), and the rain caused numerous motor vehicle accidents, but the chief effect was power outages--36,300 homes and businesses, mainly in the Sierra Nevada foothills. The figure also includes 12,000 homes and businesses in Stockton (San Joaquin county).  The KCPM television station lost a transimitter in Tehama county.  State Highway 88 through the Sierra Nevada mountains had to be closed due to the excessive snow.

Rains of 2 to 4.5 inches across El Dorado county during the early morning brought many small streams to above flood stage.  On Deer Creek near the city of Cameron Park, 10 homes were evacuated.  Further downstream, in eastern Sacramento county, the creek inundated the local area, damaging a restaurant in an historic building in the town of Sloughhouse.  The city of El Dorado's post office ended up with 4 feet of water inside the building from Slate Creek.

A powerful winter storm crippled the Reno-Carson City-Minden area over a two and a half day period.  The main portion of the storm dumped heavy snow over the region from late Friday night (20th) into early Sunday morning (22nd).  The cold moist flow continued into early Monday morning, but snowfall amounts were not as significant as on Saturday into early Sunday (in most areas).  Some noteworthy snowfall amounts over the 12-24 hour period from late Friday night into Saturday night were as follows:  6-9 inches in the lower valleys of the Greater Reno area with 10-18 inches in the western foothills, and 12-24 inches in Carson City, Washoe Valley (north of Carson City), and the Virginia City area.  Storm totals ending early Monday morning (23rd) were impressive.  The lower valleys of the Greater Reno area received from 9-12 inches with over 2 feet in the western foothills.  The Carson City area had 1-2 feet of snow.  Finally, the Virginia City area received from 4-5 feet of snow, making this winter storm the biggest in the last decade.The powerful storm paralyzed holiday travelers.  Several roads were closed while others were nearly impassable.  Numerous accidents were reported.  Approximately 16,000 homes were without power during the climax of the storm.

A powerful winter storm pummeled the Mono County area with heavy snow.  The most noteworthy snowfall accumulations were from early Saturday morning (21st) to late Saturday afternoon and also from late Saturday afternoon to Sunday afternoon.  At Mammoth Lakes, 20 inches of snow fell from early Saturday morning to late Saturday afternoon (12-18 hour period).  Also, Tom's Place (southeast of Mammoth Lakes) reported 12 inches of snow in the same time frame.  The Mammoth Lakes area received an additional 20-30 inches of snow from late Saturday afternoon to Sunday afternoon (22nd).  The storm total ending early Monday morning (23rd) was 53 inches at Mammoth Lakes with 72 inches at the Mammoth Ski Resort.

Dense fog, which reduced visibilities to as low as zero across parts of West Central and Southwest Florida during the predawn hours, gradually dissipated by mid-morning.  However, fog lingered along the immediate coastal areas of West Central Florida west of the U.S. Highway 19 corridor and north of the Tampa metropolitan area through mid-afternoon.

Low pressure produced 1 to 3 inches of rain across much of western New England during December 1 through the morning of December 2.  This amount of rainfall during the late fall season resulted in flooding across parts of Bennington and Windham Counties in southern Vermont.  In Bennington County the Walloomsac River flooded in North Bennington.  Several homes were flooded along with route 67A.  The Batten Kill at Arlington flooded with several homes affected.  Minor flooding also occurred along the Hoosic River in Bennington County.  In Windham County at Wilmington, the north branch of the Deerfield Creek flooded into nearby low lands.  No roads or houses were impacted by the flood waters.
A few large trees were down in the southern part of the county.
Strong thunderstorm winds to 69 mph ripped some siding off a house.

Thunderstorms in Fort Collins dumped heavy rain showers which resulted in widespread street flooding.  Several cars were stalled in water up to a foot deep on many streets.  Nearly 2.5 inches of rain fell in less than 2 hours.

Widespread blizzard conditions occurred as prolonged winds of 30 to 45 mph with gusts as high as 60 mph combined with heavy loose snow cover and light falling snow to produce whiteout conditions. Another storm system from the west was influenced by a strong upper level jet stream over Colorado to produce heavy snow in most mountains and some valleys of western Colorado.  6 to 12 inches of new snow were common in the mountains, while the valleys of extreme southwest Colorado and the upper Yampa River basin received 3 to 7 inches.  It was also quite windy in many areas, resulting in blowing and drifting snow.  A peak gust of 66 mph was recorded at the top of Telluride ski area.
The highway patrol reported a small tornado touched down briefly near Dillare. Damage was limited to downed trees.
Storm spotters reported 3/4 inch hail in Jonesburg.

The seasons first real blast of Arctic air moved into the state as a strong cold front dropped southeast across Iowa.  Behind the cold front, strong northwest winds of 20 to 40 MPH combined with temperatures below zero combined to produce wind chill values in the -40 to -55 degree range for nearly 24 hours.  Though there were no real problems associated with the bitter cold, it did provide Iowans a first taste of what's to come.

A band of light snow, which accompanied the first arctic front of the season, laid down a thin coating of slush which flash-froze into dangerous ice.  Numerous accidents occurred during the evening commute, including several which bottled up major arteries and interstates.  In Albemarle Co (VAZ037), 22 accidents were reported; a jackknifed tractor trailer along Interstate 66 in Warren Co (VAZ030) tied up traffic for two hours.  No deaths or serious injuries were reported.

A powerful cold front swept across central and east central Wisconsin, producing wind gusts to around 50 mph.  The strong winds tore a steel roof off of a building near Iola (Waupaca county), depositing it on top of some nearby power lines.  The winds were also responsible for destroying two construction projects, including a storage building near Marshfield (Wood county) and a brick wall of a proposed High School in Menasha (Winnebago county). Frigid arctic air surged into eastern sections of the state producing heavy upslope snow of 4 to 8 inches across the Northeast Highlands from Raton south to Las Vegas. As the air mass deepened it plunged westward through the canyons and around the central mountains (gusts to 61 mph at Cedar Crest), filling the central valleys of the Rio Grande river and spreading snow onto the plateau areas of northwest New Mexico. Several new daily record low temperatures were established. The cold was aggravated by unusually harsh wind chill which dipped to minus 20 in many areas and to a low of minus 31 degrees at Dulce in northwest Rio Arriba county. Prolonged frigid temperatures aggravated frozen water pipes, especially in the rural areas, and also prevented the usual quick thaw of snow packed and icy roads.

The remnants of Hurricane Fran moved through West Virginia on the 6th reaching northwest Pennsylvania the morning of the 7th.  The strong south to southeast winds accompanying it caused tidal flooding along Chesapeake Bay.  Flooding also extended inland along tidal sections of rivers and creeks that drain into the bay.  The tide gage at Tolchester Beach in Kent County reached 4.8 feet above mean low water.  This was a tidal departure of 2 to 2.5 feet above normal.One man was injured in Queen Anne's County in Chester.  The Kirwin Creek flooded and he received an electrical shock while fighting the flood waters in a restaurant.   Elsewhere in Queen Anne's County parts of Maryland State Route 18 were closed in Chester, Grasonville and Queenstown.  Many restaurants in Chester were closed due to flooding.  Twelve homes in the county had flooding in their crawl spaces, two had flooding up to the first floor.In Talbot County, flooding was reported in St. Michael's. The Choptank River flooded within the Daniel Crouse Memorial Park.
Trees and power lines were down and there was damage reported to several buildings near Pisgah in the southeast part of the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An early season winter storm produced a record breaking heavy wet snow in most of northeast and east central Kansas.  Accumulations ranged from 3 to 8 inches at most locations east of a line from Marysville in northwest Marshall County to Herrington in extreme southeast Dickinson County.  A few places received 9 to 11 inches.  Scattered thunderstorms locally enhanced the snowfall rates, causing amounts to vary greatly over short distances.  The National Weather Service at the Billard Airport in Topeka recorded 8.0 inches which set a new twenty-four hour and monthly snowfall record for October.  Some other specific snowfall totals included Alta Vista 11, Council Grove 8 1/2, Lawrence 8, Hiawatha 8, Oskaloosa 8, and Ottawa 6.Since leaves still remained on many trees the stress from the weight of the snow on the leaves caused extensive damage to limbs which fell onto power lines and electrical transformers.  The result was widespread power outages with more than 75,000 customers in northeast Kansas without power at the peak of the storm.  The power company which services the region estimated 2.5 million dollars of damage to its operations. The storm also contributed to numerous traffic accidents with over 100 confirmed in Topeka and Shawnee County and over 40 in Pottawatomie County.  One fatal accident occurred on US Highway 40 in Douglas County 1 mile east of Big Springs when a car collided head-on with a semi-truck.  Another fatal accident occured in Osage County along the Kansas Turnpike 20 miles southwest of Topeka when a car struck the guard rail then another vehicle that was parked along the shoulder of the highway. According to state climatological records, the year 1996 was the wettest on record (1895-present) for New Jersey.  The state-wide average was 59.97 inches, about 14.5 inches above normal.
